known_unsupported.reason: Upstream is a quantization/inference library whose OpenAI API comes from a separate server (TabbyAPI), so there is no first-party server to image; llgenie ships the ExLlamaV3 ROCm-fork engine instead.

Metal-only Apple-Silicon inference engine (incoai/splash): Metal cannot run inside llgenie's Linux image, and the Apple-Silicon platform is already served natively by the mlx engine, so a second native MLX stack would duplicate it.

Experimental C toolkit: janas-server speaks an OpenAI-style API, but its releases are Linux/Windows tarballs built by ./build.sh, its models are its own .jns format (a GGUF has to be converted first), and its README says the API and CLI change several times a week.

Apple-Silicon-only binary (brew tap or install.sh) that serves OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, but macOS 14+ on an M-series Mac is a hard requirement and Metal cannot run inside llgenie's Linux image; llgenie already ships the native mlx engine for that platform.

A desktop app, installed as an app, whose own docs describe the OpenAI endpoints its bundled llama.cpp/MLX runtimes serve; no source repository is published for the app or its serving layer, so there is nothing to build an image from and it overlaps Ollama and llama.cpp.

lse-server answers the OpenAI wire format, but upstream ships prebuilt per-platform tarballs (macOS arm64 with the notarised MacAMDGPU DriverKit runtime, Linux x86_64 needing ROCm 7) and its own HRX/Loom kernel compiler: no container recipe, and two vendor-specific runtimes to pin.

A native Mac app plus CLI (brew or pip) whose `mtplx serve` exposes OpenAI and Anthropic APIs through MLX MTP speculative decoding on Apple Silicon only; Metal cannot run in a container, and llgenie reaches that platform through its native mlx/TensorFold skills.

A desktop app and CLI delivered as platform installers, whose `magnitude server setup` runs it as a self-updating user service that tunes kernels for the local machine at install time; there is no published container image and no pinned build for llgenie to carry.

Closed-source binaries (upstream says the source comes later) behind an interactive launcher, scoped to one model on one card (Qwen3.8-27B on an RTX 5090): there is no source, release tree or image to build from.

A terminal coding agent installed from PyPI whose `openjet setup` builds llama.cpp and then JIT-compiles OpenJet's own CUDA engine for the local GPU (Qwen3.8-27B only, llama-server for every other model): it wraps llama.cpp rather than replacing it as an engine.

A model-optimisation toolkit, not a server: the OpenAI-compatible endpoint belongs to OVMS (openvinotoolkit/model_server), and OpenVINO targets Intel CPU/GPU/NPU only, so an image would add an Intel-only engine beside the llama.cpp cpu image that already runs everywhere.
A single-model (GLM-5.3-Flash) engine + dashboard built on Strata, installed by a native setup script with no container image; llgenie already ships the Strata engine for that family.

A general deep-learning framework: the MPS backend is a tensor library, and the HTTP server in front of it is a separate project (TorchServe/vLLM/SGLang). An image of PyTorch would be a Python build toolchain, not an inference server llgenie can drive for a GGUF or MLX model.

Apple-Silicon-only MLX server installed from Homebrew or PyPI, with pure MLX kernels and no Linux or GGUF path: its README scopes it to M-series Macs, calls `brew install rapid-mlx` the install, and the product it ships is a macOS desktop app plus image/video/audio generation aliases rather than a server llgenie could drive for the GGUF/MLX models it offers. Metal cannot run in llgenie's Linux image, and that platform is already served natively by the mlx engine, so a second native MLX stack would duplicate it.

A native Swift/MLX engine that streams experts from SSD on Apple Silicon, released for one model (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next MLX 4-bit) and needing macOS 14 with ~110 GB free; macOS and Metal only, so it cannot run in llgenie's Linux image.

A C++/CUDA tensor runtime loaded as libsonicboom.so through a stable C ABI (Guile first-class, no Python), verified end to end on two GGUF families; it is GPL-3.0-or-later and a library rather than a server, so llgenie has no endpoint to image and drive.

Auto-registered CUDA engine (invergent-ai/surogate, Apache-2.0, C++/CUDA): a native OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible server with a manylinux CUDA wheel, but it was auto-registered from a single announced tweet with one stated run (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B at 35.2 t/s on RTX 5090, 2026-11-01) and ships no llgenie skill/image yet. Deferred pending a ship decision tracked by #1962, consistent with how a just-listed engine with no artifact ages into the queue.

An agent harness with its own inference engine, installed by two commands on a DGX Spark and measured only there (one NVIDIA GB10 box); the engine is AGPL-3.0-only or commercial, so it is a single-box product rather than an engine llgenie can ship for every host.

It publishes container images and an OpenAI-compatible server, but it is a datacenter serving stack (GB200, MI355X; tensor and expert parallelism) tuned for 100B-2.4T models, not the single-GPU GGUF path llgenie drives on a reader's card.
A single-model (GLM-5.3-Flash EXL3) offload engine for one 24 GB card, built on SGLang + ExLlamaV3 - both of which llgenie already ships; a skill for it would duplicate two engines for one model.
A llama.cpp fork tuned for Ampere cards only: llgenie ships stock llama.cpp plus the Prism and LaurentZuijdwijk forks, and a third fork is a permanent maintenance burden for a per-card gain.

The registry names stock ggml-org/llama.cpp, which llgenie already ships as its llama.cpp engine, while its note describes an unnamed fork with KV-cache streaming; the source post names no repository, so there is no patch set to pin and no image to build.

A patch series on JigSawPT's dsv41-porte llama.cpp branch that streams DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's experts from NVMe on a ~20 GB GPU; the fork's own default branch carries the README, and the build it documents is Windows + CUDA 13, so no image can carry it as a general engine.

A community llama.cpp fork for one APU family (AMD Strix Halo gfx1151 / RDNA 3.5), built from source with -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151; llgenie ships stock llama.cpp plus the Prism and LaurentZuijdwijk forks, and a third per-chip fork is a permanent maintenance liability.
Upstream ships native binaries only (a brew cask plus linux CUDA tarballs), no container image, and it is an all-in-one app overlapping the MLX engine llgenie already serves natively.
Apple-Silicon server delivered as a macOS menu-bar app: Metal cannot run in a container, so it would need a native Metal skill, and llgenie already ships the `mlx` engine for that platform.
Not a server at all: a patch set that adds ExLlamaV3's EXL3 format to oMLX (pinned to one commit, single author) and rides oMLX's own server on Apple Silicon.

An OpenAI-compatible server written from scratch in HIP for exactly one chip and one model (AMD Strix Halo gfx1151 with 128 GB, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next); the container image carries that ROCm runtime only, so it is a single-APU experiment rather than a general engine.

A Swift/Metal runtime plus a macOS app and a loopback-only OpenAI server, hard-wired to one model (Gemma 4 26B-A4B) in its own .gturbo layout on macOS 26: no container image, no GGUF, and Metal cannot run inside llgenie's Linux image.

Metal-only Apple-Silicon MLX server (trymirai/uzu): Metal cannot run inside llgenie's Linux image, and the Apple-Silicon platform is already served natively by the mlx engine, so a second native MLX stack would duplicate it.
